'''''Cotoneaster salicifolius''''', the '''willow-leaved cotoneaster''', is a drought-tolerant, [[evergreen]] to semi-evergreen, low-lying, small to medium-sized [[shrub]] with an arched branching habit. Specimens growing in the wild, however, are generally larger, averaging five meters in height. Although native to the mountains, [[mixed forest]]s, and open places in [[western China]], it is commonly cultivated in temperate climates worldwide. [[Cultivars]] have been bred in a variety of forms, as ornamental [[groundcovers]] or shrubs.

== Description ==
The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] of the willow-leaved cotoneaster is gray-brown, its [[Plant stem|stems]] are thin, and its [[root]] system is sparse.<ref name=uconn>{{ cite web |url=http://www.hort.uconn.edu/plants/c/cotsal/cotsal3.html |title=Cotoneaster salicifolius |work=Mark H. Brand |publisher=[[University of Connecticut]] Plant Database |date=June 15, 2001 |accessdate=March 24, 2009 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080705190953/http://www.hort.uconn.edu/plants/c/cotsal/cotsal3.html |archivedate=July 5, 2008 }}</ref>

The [[foliage|leaves]] are alternate, simple, long, [[lanceolate]], dark green and resemble those of [[willow]] trees (thus the common name), and have fine gray hairs on their undersides.<ref name=uconn/> The scientific name 'salicifolius', described by the botanist [[Adrien René Franchet|Franchet]], means 'with leaves like willows' (see: Genus ''[[Salix]]''). During the colder months, they turn maroonish in color.<ref name=uconn/><ref name=ncsu>{{ cite web |url=http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/deps/horts/consumer/factsheets/groundcover/Cotoneaster_salicifolius.html |archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20110606144557/http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/factsheets/groundcover/cotoneaster_salicifolius.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 6, 2011 |title=Ground Covers: Cotoneaster salicifolius |work=Erv Evans-Consumer Horticulturist |publisher=[[North Carolina State University]] Cooperative Extension Service |date= |accessdate=March 24, 2009 }}</ref>

In June it bears many flowered, compound [[corymbs]] of white, 5–6 mm [[flowers]].<ref name=FOC1>{{ cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200010777 |title=Cotoneaster salicifolius |work= |publisher=[[Flora of China (series)|Flora of China]] |date= |accessdate=March 24, 2009}}</ref> The [[fruit]] grow as small, showy, [[apple]]-like, red [[pome]]s, ripening in September to October, and enduring into the winter.<ref name=ncsu/><ref name=msu>{{ cite web |url=http://web1.msue.msu.edu/imp/modzz/00000447.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051101114407/http://web1.msue.msu.edu/imp/modzz/00000447.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 1, 2005 |title=Cotoneaster salicifolius -- Willowleaf Cotoneaster |publisher=[[Michigan State University]] Extension |date=January 19, 2000 |accessdate=March 24, 2009 }}</ref>

The [[diploid]] [[chromosome|chromosomal]] number is 34 (2n=34).<ref name=FOC1/>

== Cultivation ==
Depending on the characteristics of the cultivar, the Willow-leaved Cotoneaster can be used as a [[hedge]] or [[windbreak|screen]]; a bank cover; in small groupings or large masses; or anywhere its colorful fall foliage or bright red fruit would direct the eye towards a focal point, or serve as a centerpiece in a garden setting.<ref name=uconn/>

=== Pests ===
''Cotoneaster salicifolius'' is susceptible to bouts with [[leaf spot]], [[scale insects]] and [[spider mites]].<ref name=uconn/> It is also considered highly susceptible to the [[Enterobacteriaceae|Enterobacteria]] [[fire blight]]<ref name = uconn/> and has been used as a test species to trial new methods of control.<ref>

(ISHS) 489:577-582 Accessed: March 25, 2009</ref> In parts of [[Europe]] where fire blight was previously unknown, cultivated specimens of this species are among the first plants identified as infected.<ref>

== List of cultivars ==
This plant has many [[cultivar]]s, ranging from tiny [[groundcover]]s to large [[shrub]]s, which include:-
{{div col|colwidth=20em}} 
* 'Angustus'
* 'Autumn Fire' or 'Herbstfeuer' (German): it grows 2 to 3 feet tall<ref name=ncsu/> <!-- Note: sources cited here seem to disagree (see entry for 'Herbstfeuer', below.) -->
*'Avonbank'
*'Avondrood': equivalent to, or thought to be equivalent to 'Repandens' and 'Repens'<ref name=uconn/><ref name=deel6>{{ cite web |url=http://www.plantago.nl/plantindex/plants/c/Cotoneaster/Cotoneaster.html?deel=6 |title=PlantIndex: Planten Geslacht Cotoneaster (pp.6) |work=Compiled by R.Koot |publisher=Plantago |date= |accessdate=March 25, 2009}}</ref><!-- Note:deel6 indicates equivalency while uconn indicates only possible equivalency. -->
*'Dekor'
* 'Dortmund': thought to be equivalent to 'Repandens' and 'Repens', and possibly to 'Avondrood'<ref name=uconn/><ref name=deel6/>
*'Emerald Carpet' or 'Green Carpet': a cultivar with denser than average foliage, it is similar to 'Repens'<ref name=uconn/><ref name=ncsu/>
*'Exburyensis'
*'Floccosus'
*'Gnom' or 'Gnome': it grows 8 to 12 inches tall<ref name=ncsu/>
*'Henryanus'
* 'Herbstfeuer' (German) or 'Autumn Fire': a cultivar that virtually lies on the ground and stands less than a foot high<ref name=msu/> <!-- Note: sources cited here seem to disagree (see entry for 'Autumn Fire', above). -->
*'HQ' : similar to "Repens"<ref name=uconn/>
*'Klampen'
*'Moner': developed in [[Monrovia]], it is thought to be the same as 'Emerald Carpet'. It grows about a foot high, and spreads 6 to 8 feet, with a compact growth habit.<ref name=msu/>
*'Mlynany
*'October Glory'
*'Parkteppich'
*'Pendulus' or 'Hybridus Pendulus'
*'Perkeo'
*'Pink Champagne'
*'Red Flare'
*'Repens' or 'Repandens' or 'Avondrood': this cultivar grows low to the ground to about 2 feet high and 8 feet wide with glossy leaves that may be semi-evergreen during excessively cold winters, but evergreen in warmer climes<ref name=uconn/><ref name=msu/>
*'Rothschildianus'
*'Rugosus' or 'Hylmoei'
*'Saldam'
*'Salicifolius'
*'Scarlet Leader': this popular, disease-resistant cultivar is ground-hugging and makes a good groundcover. In the autumn the dense, green foliage russets. It grows 2 to 3 feet tall, and 6 to 8 feet wide.<ref name=uconn/><ref name=ncsu/><ref name=msu/>
*'September Beauty'
*'Sympatie'
*'Valkenburg'
*'Willeke'
{{div col end}}
